name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q01 - Ancient Indian chemistry texts and their contributions

questiontext.text:
Match the ancient Indian texts or treatises listed in List-I with their respective chemical or technological contributions described in List-II:

List-I (Treatise / Text)List-II (Contribution / Description)
(A) Rasaratnakara(p) Indigenous methods of preparing alkalis (kshar)
(B) Rasarnavam(q) Earliest Ayurvedic treatise on medicine mentioning reduction of particle size of metals
(C) Charaka Samhita(r) Work of Nagarjuna dealing with formulation of mercury compounds and extraction of metals
(D) Sushruta Samhita(s) Tantric text discussing the use of various furnaces, ovens, and crucibles

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the contribution of Rasaratnakara
Rasaratnakara is a seminal alchemical work authored by Nagarjuna that deals comprehensively with the formulation of mercury compounds and methods for the extraction and metallurgy of metals such as gold, silver, tin, and copper. Thus, Rasaratnakara pairs with the work of Nagarjuna dealing with formulation of mercury compounds and extraction of metals.

Step 2: Determine the contribution of Rasarnavam
Rasarnavam is a prominent Tantric text dating to approximately 800 CE that describes the construction and operational use of various furnaces, ovens, crucibles, and flame coloration tests. Thus, Rasarnavam pairs with the Tantric text discussing the use of various furnaces, ovens, and crucibles.

Step 3: Determine the contribution of Charaka Samhita
Charaka Samhita is the oldest surviving Ayurvedic treatise on internal medicine that details the preparation of bhasmas and the medicinal reduction of particle size of metals. Thus, Charaka Samhita pairs with the earliest Ayurvedic treatise on medicine mentioning reduction of particle size of metals.

Step 4: Determine the contribution of Sushruta Samhita
Sushruta Samhita is an ancient Ayurvedic surgical treatise that describes indigenous methods for the preparation and therapeutic application of alkalis (kshar). Thus, Sushruta Samhita pairs with the indigenous methods of preparing alkalis (kshar).

Step 5: Final conclusion
Combining these evaluations, the verified pairings are: Rasaratnakara corresponds to (r), Rasarnavam corresponds to (s), Charaka Samhita corresponds to (q), and Sushruta Samhita corresponds to (p). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(r), B-(s), C-(q), D-(p).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q02 - SI base physical quantities and their fundamental units

questiontext.text:
Match the physical quantities in List-I with their corresponding SI base units in List-II:

List-I (Physical Quantity)List-II (SI Base Unit)
(A) Amount of substance(p) Candela (\(\text{cd}\))
(B) Electric current(q) Mole (\(\text{mol}\))
(C) Luminous intensity(r) Kelvin (\(\text{K}\))
(D) Thermodynamic temperature(s) Ampere (\(\text{A}\))

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the SI unit of amount of substance
The SI base unit for the amount of substance is the mole, abbreviated as \(\text{mol}\).

Step 2: Identify the SI unit of electric current
The SI base unit for electric current is the ampere, abbreviated as \(\text{A}\).

Step 3: Identify the SI unit of luminous intensity
The SI base unit for luminous intensity is the candela, abbreviated as \(\text{cd}\).

Step 4: Identify the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature
The SI base unit for thermodynamic temperature is the kelvin, abbreviated as \(\text{K}\).

Step 5: Final conclusion
Connecting each quantity to its canonical base unit gives: amount of substance corresponds to the mole (q), electric current corresponds to the ampere (s), luminous intensity corresponds to the candela (p), and thermodynamic temperature corresponds to the kelvin (r). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(q), B-(s), C-(p), D-(r).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q03 - SI prefixes and their decimal multiplication factors

questiontext.text:
Match the SI prefixes in List-I with their decimal multiplication factors in List-II:

List-I (Prefix)List-II (Multiplication Factor)
(A) Femto(p) \(10^{-12}\)
(B) Pico(q) \(10^{9}\)
(C) Micro(r) \(10^{-15}\)
(D) Giga(s) \(10^{-6}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the factor for femto
In the International System of Units, the prefix femto denotes a factor of \(10^{-15}\).

Step 2: Identify the factor for pico
The prefix pico denotes a submultiple factor of \(10^{-12}\).

Step 3: Identify the factor for micro
The prefix micro denotes a submultiple factor of \(10^{-6}\).

Step 4: Identify the factor for giga
The prefix giga denotes a multiple factor of \(10^{9}\).

Step 5: Final conclusion
Aligning each prefix with its decimal factor yields: femto corresponds to \(10^{-15}\) (r), pico corresponds to \(10^{-12}\) (p), micro corresponds to \(10^{-6}\) (s), and giga corresponds to \(10^{9}\) (q). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(r), B-(p), C-(s), D-(q).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q04 - Laws of chemical combination and proposing scientists

questiontext.text:
Match the laws of chemical combination in List-I with the scientists who proposed or formulated them in List-II:

List-I (Law of Chemical Combination)List-II (Formulated By)
(A) Law of Conservation of Mass(p) Joseph Proust (1799)
(B) Law of Definite Proportions(q) John Dalton (1803)
(C) Law of Multiple Proportions(r) Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac (1808)
(D) Law of Gaseous Volumes(s) Antoine Lavoisier (1789)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Associate Law of Conservation of Mass
The Law of Conservation of Mass states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. It was experimentally established by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789.

Step 2: Associate Law of Definite Proportions
The Law of Definite Proportions states that a given compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by weight. It was formulated by Joseph Proust in 1799.

Step 3: Associate Law of Multiple Proportions
The Law of Multiple Proportions states that when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in the ratio of small whole numbers. It was proposed by John Dalton in 1803.

Step 4: Associate Law of Gaseous Volumes
The Law of Gaseous Volumes states that when gases react together, they do so in volumes which bear a simple whole-number ratio to one another and to the volumes of the gaseous products, provided all measurements are made under identical conditions of temperature and pressure. It was discovered by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac in 1808.

Step 5: Final conclusion
Matching each fundamental law with its originator gives: Law of Conservation of Mass corresponds to Antoine Lavoisier (s), Law of Definite Proportions corresponds to Joseph Proust (p), Law of Multiple Proportions corresponds to John Dalton (q), and Law of Gaseous Volumes corresponds to Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac (r). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(s), B-(p), C-(q), D-(r).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q05 - Classification of matter and illustrative chemical examples

questiontext.text:
Match the classifications of matter in List-I with their illustrative examples in List-II:

List-I (Classification of Matter)List-II (Illustrative Example)
(A) Homogeneous mixture(p) Completely dissolved aqueous glucose solution
(B) Heterogeneous mixture(q) Solid mixture of sodium chloride and grain particles
(C) Chemical element(r) Chemically pure copper wire
(D) Pure compound(s) Stoichiometric crystalline water ice

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify homogeneous mixture
A homogeneous mixture possesses a uniform composition and appearance throughout its bulk. An aqueous solution of glucose in water has its solute particles uniformly distributed at the molecular level, forming a single phase. Thus, it is a homogeneous mixture.

Step 2: Identify heterogeneous mixture
A heterogeneous mixture consists of two or more distinct phases with non-uniform composition. A mixture of solid grains and sodium chloride salt exhibits visible boundaries and variable local proportions. Thus, it is a heterogeneous mixture.

Step 3: Identify chemical element
An element consists of only one type of atom and cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions. Pure copper wire is composed entirely of copper atoms. Thus, it represents an element.

Step 4: Identify pure compound
A compound is composed of two or more different elements combined in a fixed ratio by mass with distinct chemical properties. Ice consists of water molecules with hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed \(1:8\) mass ratio. Thus, it represents a pure compound.

Step 5: Final conclusion
Matching each category of matter with its appropriate representative gives: homogeneous mixture corresponds to aqueous glucose solution (p), heterogeneous mixture corresponds to sodium chloride and grain mixture (q), chemical element corresponds to pure copper wire (r), and pure compound corresponds to water ice (s). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(p), B-(q), C-(r), D-(s).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q06 - Solution concentration terms and their defining expressions

questiontext.text:
Match the concentration expressions in List-I with their precise defining characteristics in List-II:

List-I (Concentration Term)List-II (Defining Characteristic)
(A) Molarity(p) Dimensionless ratio of moles of a component to the total moles of all components
(B) Molality(q) Mass of solute present in \(100\text{ g}\) of solution
(C) Mole fraction(r) Number of moles of solute dissolved in \(1\text{ L}\) of solution; temperature-dependent
(D) Mass per cent(s) Number of moles of solute dissolved in \(1\text{ kg}\) of solvent; temperature-independent

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate Molarity
Molarity is defined as the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution: \(M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}(\text{L})}\). Because volume expands or contracts with changes in temperature, molarity is inherently temperature-dependent.

Step 2: Evaluate Molality
Molality is defined as the number of moles of solute present in one kilogram of solvent: \(m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{w_{\text{solvent}}(\text{kg})}\). Since mass is invariant with temperature, molality is temperature-independent.

Step 3: Evaluate Mole fraction
Mole fraction is defined as the ratio of the number of moles of a particular component to the total number of moles of all constituents present in the mixture: \(\chi_i = \frac{n_i}{\sum n}\). It is a dimensionless quantity.

Step 4: Evaluate Mass per cent
Mass per cent is defined as the mass of solute present per hundred grams of solution: \(\text{Mass \%} = \frac{\text{Mass of solute}}{\text{Total mass of solution}} \times 100\).

Step 5: Final conclusion
Correlating each concentration unit to its precise definition gives: molarity corresponds to (r), molality corresponds to (s), mole fraction corresponds to (p), and mass per cent corresponds to (q). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(r), B-(s), C-(p), D-(q).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q07 - Numerical measurements and their significant figure counts

questiontext.text:
Match the numerical values or counted quantities in List-I with their exact number of significant figures in List-II:

List-I (Measurement / Quantity)List-II (Number of Significant Figures)
(A) \(0.0025\)(p) 5
(B) \(2.005\)(q) 2
(C) \(500.00\)(r) Infinite
(D) \(20\text{ apples}\)(s) 4

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Count significant figures in 0.0025
Zeros preceding the first non-zero digit are leading zeros that serve only to indicate the decimal point and are not significant. In \(0.0025\), the leading zeros are insignificant, leaving only the digits \(2\) and \(5\). Hence, there are \(2\) significant figures.

Step 2: Count significant figures in 2.005
Zeros lying between two non-zero digits are always significant. In \(2.005\), the two zeros between \(2\) and \(5\) are significant. Hence, there are \(4\) significant figures.

Step 3: Count significant figures in 500.00
Trailing zeros in a number that contains a decimal point are significant. In \(500.00\), both the zeros after the decimal point and the zeros between the non-zero digit and the decimal point are significant. Hence, there are \(5\) significant figures.

Step 4: Count significant figures in 20 apples
Counting numbers of distinct discrete objects represent exact numbers with zero uncertainty. Exact numbers can be represented with an infinite number of significant figures by appending decimal zeros (such as \(20.000...\)). Hence, exact counted items possess infinite significant figures.

Step 5: Final conclusion
Matching each quantity with its significant figure count gives: \(0.0025\) corresponds to \(2\) (q), \(2.005\) corresponds to \(4\) (s), \(500.00\) corresponds to \(5\) (p), and \(20\text{ apples}\) corresponds to infinite (r). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(q), B-(s), C-(p), D-(r).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q08 - Substance quantities and total constituent particle counts

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical quantities given in List-I with the total number of constituent atoms or molecules in List-II (Take Avogadro constant \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), atomic mass of \(\text{He} = 4\text{ u}\), molar mass of \(\text{H}_2\text{O} = 18.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)):

List-I (Sample Quantity)List-II (Total Number of Particles)
(A) \(52\text{ moles of Ar}\)(p) \(13\text{ atoms}\)
(B) \(52\text{ u of He}\)(q) \(1.807 \times 10^{24}\text{ molecules}\)
(C) \(52\text{ g of He}\)(r) \(3.131 \times 10^{25}\text{ atoms}\)
(D) \(54\text{ g of }\text{H}_2\text{O}\)(s) \(7.829 \times 10^{24}\text{ atoms}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate atoms in 52 moles of Ar
Argon is a monoatomic noble gas. One mole of argon contains \(N_A\) atoms: \[ N = n \times N_A = 52\text{ mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 3.131 \times 10^{25}\text{ atoms} \]

Step 2: Calculate atoms in 52 u of He
A single helium atom has a mass of \(4\text{ u}\). The total number of helium atoms is: \[ N = \frac{\text{Total mass in u}}{\text{Mass of one atom in u}} = \frac{52\text{ u}}{4\text{ u/atom}} = 13\text{ atoms} \]

Step 3: Calculate atoms in 52 g of He
The molar mass of helium is \(4\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). The number of moles is: \[ n = \frac{52\text{ g}}{4\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 13\text{ mol} \] The total number of atoms is: \[ N = 13\text{ mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 7.8286 \times 10^{24} \approx 7.829 \times 10^{24}\text{ atoms} \]

Step 4: Calculate molecules in 54 g of H2O
The molar mass of water (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\)) is \(18.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). The number of moles of water is: \[ n = \frac{54\text{ g}}{18.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 3.0\text{ mol} \] The total number of water molecules is: \[ N = 3.0\text{ mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 1.8066 \times 10^{24} \approx 1.807 \times 10^{24}\text{ molecules} \]

Step 5: Final conclusion
Matching each sample to its particle count gives: \(52\text{ moles of Ar}\) corresponds to \(3.131 \times 10^{25}\text{ atoms}\) (r), \(52\text{ u of He}\) corresponds to \(13\text{ atoms}\) (p), \(52\text{ g of He}\) corresponds to \(7.829 \times 10^{24}\text{ atoms}\) (s), and \(54\text{ g of }\text{H}_2\text{O}\) corresponds to \(1.807 \times 10^{24}\text{ molecules}\) (q). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(r), B-(p), C-(s), D-(q).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q09 - Stoichiometric chemical processes and quantitative outcomes

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical processes or reaction systems in List-I with their stoichiometric or quantitative outcomes in List-II:

List-I (Process / Reaction System)List-II (Quantitative Outcome)
(A) Complete combustion of \(16.0\text{ g}\) of methane (\(\text{CH}_4\))(p) Produces \(36.0\text{ g}\) of water
(B) Reaction of \(50.0\text{ kg}\) of \(\text{N}_2\) with \(10.0\text{ kg}\) of \(\text{H}_2\) to form ammonia(q) Dihydrogen gas acts as the limiting reagent
(C) Dissolving \(4.0\text{ g}\) of \(\text{NaOH}\) in water to form \(250\text{ mL}\) of solution(r) Yields a solution of molarity \(0.40\text{ M}\)
(D) Thermal decomposition of \(20.0\text{ g}\) of pure \(\text{CaCO}_3\)(s) Produces \(8.80\text{ g}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\) gas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze combustion of methane
The balanced chemical equation is: \[ \text{CH}_4(g) + 2\text{O}_2(g) \to \text{CO}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \] Molar mass of \(\text{CH}_4 = 16.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), so \(16.0\text{ g}\) is \(1.0\text{ mol}\). According to stoichiometry, \(1.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{CH}_4\) yields \(2.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\). With the molar mass of water being \(18.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), mass of water produced is: \[ 2.0\text{ mol} \times 18.0\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 36.0\text{ g} \]

Step 2: Analyze reaction of N2 and H2
The balanced equation is \(\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \to 2\text{NH}_3(g)\). Number of moles of \(\text{N}_2 = \frac{50.0 \times 10^3\text{ g}}{28.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 1.786 \times 10^3\text{ mol}\). Number of moles of \(\text{H}_2 = \frac{10.0 \times 10^3\text{ g}}{2.016\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 4.960 \times 10^3\text{ mol}\). Stoichiometry requires \(3\) moles of \(\text{H}_2\) per mole of \(\text{N}_2\). For \(1.786 \times 10^3\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{N}_2\), the required amount of \(\text{H}_2\) is: \[ 3 \times 1.786 \times 10^3\text{ mol} = 5.358 \times 10^3\text{ mol} \] Since only \(4.960 \times 10^3\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\) is available, dihydrogen gas is completely consumed first and acts as the limiting reagent.

Step 3: Analyze molarity of NaOH solution
Molar mass of \(\text{NaOH} = 23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). Moles of \(\text{NaOH} = \frac{4.0\text{ g}}{40.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.10\text{ mol}\). Volume of solution in litres is \(250\text{ mL} = 0.250\text{ L}\). Molarity is: \[ M = \frac{0.10\text{ mol}}{0.250\text{ L}} = 0.40\text{ mol L}^{-1} = 0.40\text{ M} \]

Step 4: Analyze decomposition of CaCO3
The decomposition reaction is \(\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\). Molar mass of \(\text{CaCO}_3 = 40.0 + 12.0 + 48.0 = 100.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). Moles of \(\text{CaCO}_3 = \frac{20.0\text{ g}}{100.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.20\text{ mol}\). According to stoichiometry, \(0.20\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{CaCO}_3\) produces \(0.20\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\). Molar mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 44.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). The mass of \(\text{CO}_2\) formed is: \[ 0.20\text{ mol} \times 44.0\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 8.80\text{ g} \]

Step 5: Final conclusion
Matching each process to its outcome shows: combustion of \(16.0\text{ g}\) methane corresponds to producing \(36.0\text{ g}\) water (p), reaction of \(50.0\text{ kg}\) \(\text{N}_2\) with \(10.0\text{ kg}\) \(\text{H}_2\) corresponds to dihydrogen acting as the limiting reagent (q), dissolving \(4.0\text{ g}\) \(\text{NaOH}\) in \(250\text{ mL}\) corresponds to a molarity of \(0.40\text{ M}\) (r), and decomposition of \(20.0\text{ g}\) \(\text{CaCO}_3\) corresponds to forming \(8.80\text{ g}\) \(\text{CO}_2\) (s). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(p), B-(q), C-(r), D-(s).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOMEBASICCONCEPTSOFCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_Q10 - Chemical compounds and constituent element mass percentages

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical compounds and designated elements in List-I with their calculated mass percentages in List-II (Take atomic masses: \(\text{H} = 1.008\text{ u}\), \(\text{C} = 12.01\text{ u}\), \(\text{O} = 16.00\text{ u}\), \(\text{Fe} = 55.85\text{ u}\)):

List-I (Compound and Target Element)List-II (Mass Percentage of Element)
(A) Hydrogen in water (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\))(p) \(52.14\%\)
(B) Carbon in ethanol (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\))(q) \(11.18\%\)
(C) Iron in iron(III) oxide (\(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\))(r) \(72.71\%\)
(D) Oxygen in carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\))(s) \(69.94\%\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate mass percentage of hydrogen in water
Molar mass of \(\text{H}_2\text{O} = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). Mass of hydrogen in one mole is \(2 \times 1.008 = 2.016\text{ g}\). Mass percentage is: \[ \text{Mass \% H} = \frac{2.016}{18.016} \times 100 = 11.1898\% \approx 11.18\% \]

Step 2: Calculate mass percentage of carbon in ethanol
Molecular formula of ethanol is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\) (or \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}\)). Molar mass \(= 2(12.01) + 6(1.008) + 16.00 = 24.02 + 6.048 + 16.00 = 46.068\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). Mass of carbon is \(24.02\text{ g}\). Mass percentage is: \[ \text{Mass \% C} = \frac{24.02}{46.068} \times 100 = 52.140\% \approx 52.14\% \]

Step 3: Calculate mass percentage of iron in iron(III) oxide
Molar mass of \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 = 2(55.85) + 3(16.00) = 111.70 + 48.00 = 159.70\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). Mass of iron is \(111.70\text{ g}\). Mass percentage is: \[ \text{Mass \% Fe} = \frac{111.70}{159.70} \times 100 = 69.9436\% \approx 69.94\% \]

Step 4: Calculate mass percentage of oxygen in carbon dioxide
Molar mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). Mass of oxygen is \(32.00\text{ g}\). Mass percentage is: \[ \text{Mass \% O} = \frac{32.00}{44.01} \times 100 = 72.7107\% \approx 72.71\% \]

Step 5: Final conclusion
Matching each compound with its constituent percentage shows: hydrogen in \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) corresponds to \(11.18\%\) (q), carbon in ethanol corresponds to \(52.14\%\) (p), iron in \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\) corresponds to \(69.94\%\) (s), and oxygen in \(\text{CO}_2\) corresponds to \(72.71\%\) (r). Therefore, the correct matching sequence is A-(q), B-(p), C-(s), D-(r).
